title: AI risks give QBE pause for thought
full_text:
Insurers should be careful rushing into novel areas of cover such as cyber security, because artificial-intelligence models could be harnessed by criminals and unleash a torrent of claims, QBE’s chief executive has warned.
Ruling off a $US1.03bn ($1.4bn) interim profit, up from the $US997m, QBE chief executive Andrew Horton reflected upon the strengths of the insurer’s overseas business.
He said the Australian division is under pressure, with sluggish growth prospects and a potential glut of investment from overseas insurers pushing down premiums.
QBE told investors it was on track to deliver growth “in the mid single digits” for the full-year.
This is after QBE grew its insurance operation by 6 per cent to $US15.1bn, up from $US13.8bn, writing business across North America, Australia, and several countries in Europe and Asia.
Mr Horton told The Australian data centres were a key target area for QBE, which has assembled a team out of its London operation as specialists in the area.
He noted the different insurance needed when building and separately running data centres.
Mr Horton said this approach would be a test of the many years he’d spent co-ordinating QBE’s different teams across geographical markets.
There could yet be an oversupply of AI-related technology projects into the market, noting QBE would be circumspect in how many policies it writes for data centre customers.
“We’ve got to not go all-in on them,” Mr Horton said. “Think about how much capacity we put down on them. It should be consistent with any insurance portfolio.” QBE is also looking to grow its cyber insurance division, but Mr Horton warned this came with its own risks.
AI models could make hacking far easier, triggering a raft of claims at insurers’ expense.
“We’ve got to be very thoughtful about how much cyber business to write. You don’t want to bet the whole company on it and find a lot more claims,” Mr Horton said. “We don’t want to give up on our insureds if we think the risk is too great.” QBE is facing uneven growth prospects for its business. Its Australian operations contracted by 1 per cent, excluding price rises, over the first six months of the 2026 financial year.
QBE’s international book meanwhile rose 11 per cent in size over the same period. Its North American operations were up 4 per cent.
“It’s tough to grow here in Australia, the market is incredibly competitive,” Mr Horton said.
The QBE boss noted how Australia was an attractive market to write cover. “Everyone loves operating here,” he said. “Not many of us realise the market is not that big.” QBE’s interim result was bolstered by a beneficial catastrophe exposure, with claims of $US445m, well below its first half budget of $US517m.
This reflected QBE largely avoiding claims for hail, floods and storms that have otherwise blighted Australian general insurers Suncorp and IAG.
QBE’s Australian arm, which represents nearly a third of its business, nonetheless copped $US218m in catastrophe claims.
On Mr Horton’s watch, QBE has also walked away from its former insurance operations writing cover for mid-market American customers. QBE sold most of those old policies.
On Friday, it announced it would sell a $1.6bn of portfolio of premiums. Mr Horton said this had given QBE “consistency” assuming the marker of a good insurer was not just what it did cover, but also “what they don’t do”.
“I felt we were writing too much business that wasn’t performing very well,” he said.
QBE is also expecting to complete the sale of its trade credit business in the second half of the financial year. An interim 33c dividend was declared, representing 33 per cent of profit. Shares in QBE fell 1.62 per cent, closing at $23.09.
